span.label: terminology theory itself - the several accounts of what a term is, what a concept is, and whether the relation between them is one-to-one
span.quote: One of the basic assertions of General Terminology Theory (Wüster 1979; Felber 1984) is that terms in specialized language are inherently different from general language words because of the monosemic reference between terms and concepts. In other words, the general claim is that a term or a specialized language unit can be distinguished from a general language word by its single-meaning relationship with the specialized concept that it designates,

span.label: what the successive theories of terminology assume about terms and concepts, and which of those assumptions survive contact with how specialized language is actually used
span.quote: Terminology theory seems to be evolving from prescriptive to descriptive with a growing focus on the study of specialized language units from a social, linguistic and cognitive perspective.

span.label: a critical overview of terminology theories from Wuster's General Terminology Theory to frame-based terminology, tracing one movement - prescriptive to descriptive - and naming what each successor still cannot do
span.quote: Terminology theory seems to be evolving from prescriptive to descriptive with a growing focus on the study of specialized language units from a social, linguistic and cognitive perspective.

span.label: critique
span.quote: However, this is an extremely idealized vision of specialized communication. Even the most cursory examination of specialized language texts shows that terminological variation is quite frequent, and that such variation seems to stem from parameters of specialized communication, such as the knowledge and prestige of the speakers, text function, text content, etc. The same concept can often be designated by more than one term, and the same linguistic form can be used to refer to more than one concept.

span.label: a founding theory that required one term per concept, and a literature that found polysemy, synonymy and variation everywhere it looked
span.quote: The reason for this was that the first approximations to terminology had normalization as a primary objective. Great pains were taken to strive for totally unambiguous communication through standardization. This signified univocity or one-to-one reference between term and concept. The fact that the majority of terms designate concepts that represent objects in a specialized knowledge field meant that such an objective seemed possible to achieve. Nevertheless, it soon became apparent that this was more a desideratum than a reality.

span.label: critical review of terminology theories - GTT, socioterminology, the Communicative Theory of Terminology, sociocognitive terminology and frame-based terminology - each read against what specialized translation actually needs
span.term: critical review of terminology theories - GTT, socioterminology, the Communicative Theory of Terminology, sociocognitive terminology and frame-based terminology - each read against what specialized translation actually needs
span.quote: Although for many years the GTT offered the only set of principles and premises for compiling terminological data, its rigid view of the semantics of terminological units projected a uniformly limited representation of specialized knowledge concepts without allowing for their multidimensional nature.

span.label: **THE FOUNDING THEORY REQUIRED ONE TERM PER CONCEPT.** `a term or a specialized language unit can be distinguished from a general language word BY ITS SINGLE-MEANING RELATIONSHIP with the specialized concept that it designates`
span.quote: One of the basic assertions of General Terminology Theory (Wüster 1979; Felber 1984) is that terms in specialized language are inherently different from general language words because of the monosemic reference between terms and concepts. In other words, the general claim is that a term or a specialized language unit can be distinguished from a general language word by its single-meaning relationship with the specialized concept that it designates,

span.label: and pursued it by standardization: `Great pains were taken to strive for TOTALLY UNAMBIGUOUS COMMUNICATION through standardization. This signified UNIVOCITY or one-to-one reference between term and concept ... it soon became apparent that this was MORE A DESIDERATUM THAN A REALITY`
span.quote: The reason for this was that the first approximations to terminology had normalization as a primary objective. Great pains were taken to strive for totally unambiguous communication through standardization. This signified univocity or one-to-one reference between term and concept. The fact that the majority of terms designate concepts that represent objects in a specialized knowledge field meant that such an objective seemed possible to achieve. Nevertheless, it soon became apparent that this was more a desideratum than a reality.

span.label: **THE MAPPING FAILS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE** - `The same concept can often be designated by MORE THAN ONE TERM, and the same linguistic form can be used to refer to MORE THAN ONE CONCEPT` - and the variation `seems to stem from parameters of specialized communication, such as the KNOWLEDGE AND PRESTIGE OF THE SPEAKERS`
span.quote: However, this is an extremely idealized vision of specialized communication. Even the most cursory examination of specialized language texts shows that terminological variation is quite frequent, and that such variation seems to stem from parameters of specialized communication, such as the knowledge and prestige of the speakers, text function, text content, etc. The same concept can often be designated by more than one term, and the same linguistic form can be used to refer to more than one concept.

span.label: so the target moves as well as the aim: `standardization is A CHIMERA since language is in constant change ... the use of one term instead of another can reflect the knowledge, social and professional status of a group of users, AS WELL AS THE POWER RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN SPEAKERS`
span.quote: According to socioterminologists, standardization is a chimera since language is in constant change. Polysemy and synonymy are inevitably present in terminology and specialized texts, and the use of one term instead of another can reflect the knowledge, social and professional status of a group of users, as well as the power relationships between speakers.

span.label: **AND THE OBJECT BEING CLASSIFIED DOES NOT HOLD STILL** - `Terminological variation also points to the fact that CONCEPT SYSTEMS AND DEFINITIONS ARE NOT STATIC. This is a reality that any theory that aspires to explanatory adequacy MUST DEAL WITH`
span.quote: Terminological variation also points to the fact that concept systems and definitions are not static. This is a reality that any theory that aspires to explanatory adequacy must deal with.

span.label: **THE DISCIPLINE'S INDEPENDENCE WAS BOUGHT WITH THE CLAIM** - `In its initial phase Terminology was interested in asserting its independence ... This goal led terminologists to go to great lengths to emphasize differences between the two EVEN TO THE EXTENT OF AFFIRMING THAT TERMS ARE NOT WORDS`
span.quote: In its initial phase Terminology was interested in asserting its independence from other knowledge areas, and creating a totally independent discipline. This goal led terminologists to go to great lengths to emphasize differences between the two even to the extent of affirming that terms are not words.

span.label: and the successors give it up: frame-based terminology `maintains that trying to find A DISTINCTION BETWEEN TERMS AND WORDS IS NO LONGER FRUITFUL OR EVEN VIABLE, and that the best way to study specialized knowledge units is BY STUDYING THEIR BEHAVIOR IN TEXTS`
span.quote: For example, it also maintains that trying to find a distinction between terms and words is no longer fruitful or even viable, and that the best way to study specialized knowledge units is by studying their behavior in texts.

span.label: **AND THE DEFINITIONS STOP BEING COPIED AND START BEING DERIVED** - `Such definitions are NOT ENTERED IN A CUT-AND-PASTE FASHION from other resources. Rather they are BASED ON THE DATA EXTRACTED FROM CORPUS ANALYSIS`
span.quote: Such definitions are not entered in a cut-and-paste fashion from other resources. Rather they are based on the data extracted from corpus analysis, which is the main source of paradigmatic and syntagmatic information about the term.

span.label: **THE PAPER SAYS THE CATEGORY HAS NO AGREED CONTENT** - `the structure of categories is a recurrent topic, and in this sense there have been many proposals regarding their organization. In the final analysis, however, THE ONLY CONSENSUS IS THAT A CATEGORY CAN BE VIRTUALLY ANYTHING`
span.quote: Indeed, the structure of categories is a recurrent topic, and in this sense there have been many proposals regarding their organization (Green & Evans 2006). In the final analysis, however, the only consensus is that a category can be virtually anything.

span.label: and that the structures are built by intuition and blessed afterwards - `in even the best terminology manuals, the question of HOW to develop such configurations is NEVER TRULY EXPLAINED, and as a general rule, they are regarded as A PRODUCT OF THE TERMINOLOGIST'S INTUITION, WHICH IS AFTERWARDS VALIDATED BY CONSULTATION WITH EXPERTS`
span.quote: It is unfortunate that this focus has not as yet been accompanied by a systematic reflection on how to elaborate, design, and organize such a structure. For example, in even the best terminology manuals, the question of how to develop such configurations is never truly explained, and as a general rule, they are regarded as a product of the terminologist’s intuition, which is afterwards validated by consultation with experts.

span.label: **THE PROTOTYPE MODEL IS REJECTED FOR A REASON THAT APPLIES TO ANY HAND-BUILT ONTOLOGY** - prototypes `are NOT VIABLE as a mode of category organization because at the end of the day they DEPEND ON THE SUBJECTIVE EVALUATION OF THE TERMINOLOGIST. It is IMPOSSIBLE to define the exact nature of the center of prototypical categories or explain how degrees of prototypicality can be OBJECTIVELY MEASURED`
span.quote: This seems to point to the fact that prototypes, despite being a very seductive concept, are not viable as a mode of category organization because at the end of the day they depend on the subjective evaluation of the terminologist. It is impossible to define the exact nature of the center of prototypical categories or explain how degrees of prototypicality can be objectively measured.

span.label: with the same charge laid against idealized cognitive models: they are `TOTALLY UNCONSTRAINED`, based on `AN OPEN-ENDED INVENTORY OF CONCEPTUAL RELATIONS`, and the result `seems to be LARGELY BASED ON THE INTUITION OF THE MODELER`
span.quote: Clear disadvantages of such representations are the fact that: (1) they are totally unconstrained; (2) they are based on an open-ended inventory of conceptual relations; (3) the resulting ICM and/or prototypical category seems to be largely based on the intuition of the modeler.

span.label: **and `domain` is ambiguous in the discipline that depends on it most** - it `sometimes refers to the KNOWLEDGE AREA ITSELF, and other times, refers to the CATEGORIES OF CONCEPTS within the specialized field`, and which one is meant `has DRAMATIC CONSEQUENCES for its internal structure`
span.quote: Regarding conceptual domains, in Terminology there seem to be two views on the matter, which are not necessarily incompatible with each other. A domain sometimes refers to the knowledge area itself, and other times, refers to the categories of concepts within the specialized field. Evidently, whether a domain is defined as one or the other has dramatic consequences for its internal structure.

span.label: This is a critical review, not a study: no corpus is measured, no theory is tested, and the judgements between theories - including that the CTT's relation to Linguistics is `A LIGHT FLIRTATION with various models rather than a MONOGAMOUS RELATIONSHIP with any one` - are the author's readings, argued rather than evidenced
span.quote: Despite its clear description of the nature of terminological units and the fact that it mentions a term’s “syntactic structure and valence”, the CTT avoids opting for any specific linguistic model. The relation of the CTT with Linguistics is more in the nature of a light flirtation with various models than a monogamous relationship with any one in particular.

span.label: categorization in terminology is based on Prototype Theory, using degrees of typicality as the configurational pattern for conceptual categories
span.quote: The model of categorization in Cognitive Linguistics and sociocognitive terminology is based on Rosch’s (1978) Prototype Theory, which uses degrees of typicality as the configurational pattern for conceptual categories or domains.

span.label: frames are carried into terminology as cognitive structuring devices based on experience, providing the background knowledge that motivates the existence of words
span.quote: Frames also fall within cognitive linguistic approaches, and are a type of cognitive structuring device based on experience that provide the background knowledge and motivation for the existence of words in a language as well as the way those words are used in discourse.

span.label: reading each theory against a task it must serve - specialized translation - rather than against its own stated aims
span.note: eliminates: a theory being judged coherent on its own terms while being useless for the work; the GTT `did not even attempt to account for the syntax and pragmatics of specialized language ... it could not be usefully applied to translation` · outcome: held
span.quote: Although for many years the GTT offered the only set of principles and premises for compiling terminological data, its rigid view of the semantics of terminological units projected a uniformly limited representation of specialized knowledge concepts without allowing for their multidimensional nature.

span.label: listing the founding theory's five premises and the five rebuttals against them point for point
span.note: eliminates: a critique that argues past its target; each objection is attached to the premise it denies, so a reader can see which of the five survive · outcome: held
span.quote: 1. Concepts have a central role in regards to their linguistic designations. 2. Concepts and categories have clear-cut boundaries. 3. Terminographic definitions should always be intensional. 4. Monosemic reference is the rule in terminology, where there is a oneto-one correspondence between terms and concepts. 5. Specialized language can only be studied synchronically.

span.label: checking whether the successor theories deliver what they promise - asking the CTT how its conceptual representations are created and what constraints they have
span.note: eliminates: a replacement being credited for the ambition rather than the delivery; the answer is that the CTT `is more than a little vague` on exactly that · outcome: failed
span.quote: Although in a very general way the CTT bases its semantics on conceptual representation, it is more than a little vague when it comes to explaining how such representations are created, what they look like, and what constraints they might have:

span.label: terminology
span.quote: As has often been observed, terminology is a word that can either begin with an upper or lower-case letter. When terminology begins with a small t, it refers to the units in any specialized knowledge field. When it begins with a large T, it refers to the study of specialized language.

span.label: monosemic reference
span.quote: One of the basic assertions of General Terminology Theory (Wüster 1979; Felber 1984) is that terms in specialized language are inherently different from general language words because of the monosemic reference between terms and concepts. In other words, the general claim is that a term or a specialized language unit can be distinguished from a general language word by its single-meaning relationship with the specialized concept that it designates,

span.label: univocity
span.quote: The reason for this was that the first approximations to terminology had normalization as a primary objective. Great pains were taken to strive for totally unambiguous communication through standardization. This signified univocity or one-to-one reference between term and concept. The fact that the majority of terms designate concepts that represent objects in a specialized knowledge field meant that such an objective seemed possible to achieve. Nevertheless, it soon became apparent that this was more a desideratum than a reality.

span.label: terms
span.quote: In its initial phase Terminology was interested in asserting its independence from other knowledge areas, and creating a totally independent discipline. This goal led terminologists to go to great lengths to emphasize differences between the two even to the extent of affirming that terms are not words.

span.label: terminological variation
span.quote: However, this is an extremely idealized vision of specialized communication. Even the most cursory examination of specialized language texts shows that terminological variation is quite frequent, and that such variation seems to stem from parameters of specialized communication, such as the knowledge and prestige of the speakers, text function, text content, etc. The same concept can often be designated by more than one term, and the same linguistic form can be used to refer to more than one concept.

span.label: GTT
span.quote: Although for many years the GTT offered the only set of principles and premises for compiling terminological data, its rigid view of the semantics of terminological units projected a uniformly limited representation of specialized knowledge concepts without allowing for their multidimensional nature.

span.label: standardization
span.quote: According to socioterminologists, standardization is a chimera since language is in constant change. Polysemy and synonymy are inevitably present in terminology and specialized texts, and the use of one term instead of another can reflect the knowledge, social and professional status of a group of users, as well as the power relationships between speakers.

span.label: Theory of the Doors
span.quote: Cabré (ibid.) proposes the Theory of the Doors, a metaphor representing the possible ways of accessing, analyzing, and understanding terminological units. She compares a terminological unit to a polyhedron, a three-dimensional solid figure with a varying number of facets. Similarly, a terminological unit can also be said to have three dimensions: a cognitive dimension, a linguistic dimension, and a communicative dimension. Each is a separate door through which terminological units can be accessed. Nonetheless, one’s choice of door (or focus) does not entail a rejection of the other two perspectives, which continue to reside in the background.

span.label: prototypes
span.quote: This seems to point to the fact that prototypes, despite being a very seductive concept, are not viable as a mode of category organization because at the end of the day they depend on the subjective evaluation of the terminologist. It is impossible to define the exact nature of the center of prototypical categories or explain how degrees of prototypicality can be objectively measured.

span.label: ICM
span.quote: Clear disadvantages of such representations are the fact that: (1) they are totally unconstrained; (2) they are based on an open-ended inventory of conceptual relations; (3) the resulting ICM and/or prototypical category seems to be largely based on the intuition of the modeler.

span.label: terminological knowledge bases
span.quote: When term bases become terminological knowledge bases, as conceived by Meyer, they enhance data because the concepts and designations are linked to each other by meaningful relationships. Although the traditional generic-specific and part-whole relationships are contemplated, there is a greater emphasis on other types of relationships that enrich the resulting knowledge structure, such as cause-effect, object-function, etc. (Bowker & L’Homme 2004).

span.label: category
span.quote: Indeed, the structure of categories is a recurrent topic, and in this sense there have been many proposals regarding their organization (Green & Evans 2006). In the final analysis, however, the only consensus is that a category can be virtually anything.

span.label: domain
span.quote: Regarding conceptual domains, in Terminology there seem to be two views on the matter, which are not necessarily incompatible with each other. A domain sometimes refers to the knowledge area itself, and other times, refers to the categories of concepts within the specialized field. Evidently, whether a domain is defined as one or the other has dramatic consequences for its internal structure.

span.label: `terminology` (small t) - the units in any specialized knowledge field; `Terminology` (capital T) - the study of specialized language. The disambiguation is carried entirely by the capital letter
span.quote: As has often been observed, terminology is a word that can either begin with an upper or lower-case letter. When terminology begins with a small t, it refers to the units in any specialized knowledge field. When it begins with a large T, it refers to the study of specialized language.

span.label: `monosemic reference` - a term distinguished from a general-language word by its single-meaning relationship with the concept it designates, and by the stability of that relationship in texts
span.quote: One of the basic assertions of General Terminology Theory (Wüster 1979; Felber 1984) is that terms in specialized language are inherently different from general language words because of the monosemic reference between terms and concepts. In other words, the general claim is that a term or a specialized language unit can be distinguished from a general language word by its single-meaning relationship with the specialized concept that it designates,

span.label: `domain` - in Terminology, either the knowledge area itself OR the categories of concepts within the specialized field, with different consequences either way
span.quote: Regarding conceptual domains, in Terminology there seem to be two views on the matter, which are not necessarily incompatible with each other. A domain sometimes refers to the knowledge area itself, and other times, refers to the categories of concepts within the specialized field. Evidently, whether a domain is defined as one or the other has dramatic consequences for its internal structure.

span.label: `terminological knowledge base` (Meyer) - a term bank whose concepts and designations are linked by meaningful relationships, not only generic-specific and part-whole
span.quote: When term bases become terminological knowledge bases, as conceived by Meyer, they enhance data because the concepts and designations are linked to each other by meaningful relationships. Although the traditional generic-specific and part-whole relationships are contemplated, there is a greater emphasis on other types of relationships that enrich the resulting knowledge structure, such as cause-effect, object-function, etc. (Bowker & L’Homme 2004).

span.label: `standardization` - the founding objective of the discipline, and in socioterminology `a chimera since language is in constant change`
span.quote: According to socioterminologists, standardization is a chimera since language is in constant change. Polysemy and synonymy are inevitably present in terminology and specialized texts, and the use of one term instead of another can reflect the knowledge, social and professional status of a group of users, as well as the power relationships between speakers.

span.label: critiques → the General Terminology Theory's requirement of monosemic, one-to-one reference between terms and concepts

span.term: Theory of the Doors (Cabre) - a terminological unit as `a POLYHEDRON` with cognitive, linguistic and communicative dimensions, `each a SEPARATE DOOR` - and choosing one door `DOES NOT ENTAIL A REJECTION of the other two`
span.quote: Cabré (ibid.) proposes the Theory of the Doors, a metaphor representing the possible ways of accessing, analyzing, and understanding terminological units. She compares a terminological unit to a polyhedron, a three-dimensional solid figure with a varying number of facets. Similarly, a terminological unit can also be said to have three dimensions: a cognitive dimension, a linguistic dimension, and a communicative dimension. Each is a separate door through which terminological units can be accessed. Nonetheless, one’s choice of door (or focus) does not entail a rejection of the other two perspectives, which continue to reside in the background.

span.label: terminological knowledge base (Meyer) - concepts and designations `LINKED TO EACH OTHER BY MEANINGFUL RELATIONSHIPS`, with emphasis on relations beyond generic-specific: `cause-effect, object-function`
span.term: terminological knowledge base (Meyer) - concepts and designations `LINKED TO EACH OTHER BY MEANINGFUL RELATIONSHIPS`, with emphasis on relations beyond generic-specific: `cause-effect, object-function`
span.quote: When term bases become terminological knowledge bases, as conceived by Meyer, they enhance data because the concepts and designations are linked to each other by meaningful relationships. Although the traditional generic-specific and part-whole relationships are contemplated, there is a greater emphasis on other types of relationships that enrich the resulting knowledge structure, such as cause-effect, object-function, etc. (Bowker & L’Homme 2004).

span.label: GTT premises listed as under challenge
span.term: GTT premises listed as under challenge
span.quote: 1. Concepts have a central role in regards to their linguistic designations. 2. Concepts and categories have clear-cut boundaries. 3. Terminographic definitions should always be intensional. 4. Monosemic reference is the rule in terminology, where there is a oneto-one correspondence between terms and concepts. 5. Specialized language can only be studied synchronically.

span.label: Wuster's stated objectives
span.quote: Since Wüster believed that the function of Terminology was to create and standardize names for concepts, syntax was not regarded as falling within the scope of Terminology. Within the context of this theory, Terminology was also exclusively synchronic, and the diachronic dimension of terms was not considered. Wüster’s principal objectives (apud Cabré 2003: 173) were: 1. To eliminate ambiguity from technical languages by means of standardization of terminology in order to make them efficient tools of communication; 2. To convince all users of technical languages of the benefits of standardized terminology; 3. To establish terminology as a discipline for all practical purposes and to give it the status of a science.

span.label: There is no corpus count, no coder, no measurement anywhere in the paper. The comparisons between theories are argued - `the relation of the CTT with Linguistics is more in the nature of A LIGHT FLIRTATION with various models than a MONOGAMOUS RELATIONSHIP with any one in particular` - and **the paper's own charge against prototypes, that they rest on the terminologist's subjective evaluation, applies to its rankings too.**
span.term: **a review whose judgements are readings, and it does not pretend otherwise**
span.quote: Despite its clear description of the nature of terminological units and the fact that it mentions a term’s “syntactic structure and valence”, the CTT avoids opting for any specific linguistic model. The relation of the CTT with Linguistics is more in the nature of a light flirtation with various models than a monogamous relationship with any one in particular.
